title: Play the ball well
hook: players care about handling the ball well, not about the ball (Discourses 2.5)
carry: let the ball be the ball

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bold outside: confident about outside things, careful with your own judgments. Your line was turn the mask around.

Watch a pickup basketball game in a park. Nobody stops to argue about whether the ball is a good ball or a bad ball. It's just the ball. Everything they care about is what they do with it: the pass, the catch, the footwork, the shot. A great player with a scuffed, half-flat ball is still a joy to watch. Epictetus used ball games, and dice, to answer a hard puzzle in Stoic thought.
screen: `NOBODY ARGUES ABOUT THE BALL.` → `THE PASS, THE CATCH, THE SHOT.` → `A HARD STOIC PUZZLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the puzzle. The Stoics said outside things, money, health, even life itself, are neither good nor bad; only how we use them is. So why care about anything? Why not shrug at everything? That's Discourses book two, chapter five: how greatness of mind fits with carefulness. Epictetus answers with games. Look at people playing dice, he says. The dice and the counters don't matter, and you can't control what falls. But using well what falls is your job, and you can do it with real care. Then the ball players. None of them argues about whether the ball is good or bad. They argue about throwing and catching, and there they're all skill, speed and attention. Then a game with far more at stake. Socrates, he says, knew how to play ball, even in the court where he was tried. And what was the ball? Life. Chains. Exile. Drinking poison. Being taken from his wife, and leaving his children without a father. Those were what he was handed, and he handled them with good form. So: don't treat the ball as everything, and don't treat the game as nothing. Pour all your care into the playing. A job, a diagnosis, a family situation: those are what's been tossed to you. How you catch them and pass them on is where the skill lives.
screen: `THE PUZZLE: WHY CARE?` · `THE DICE DON'T MATTER, THE PLAY DOES.` · `SOCRATES KNEW HOW TO PLAY BALL.` · `ALL YOUR CARE GOES INTO THE PLAYING.` · then, large: `PLAY THE BALL WELL.`

segments.voice: Think of one task waiting for you today, ordinary or hard, and notice what you're hoping it gets you: praise, a result, a relief. That's the ball; set it down for now. Then picture doing the task itself with full care, the first step, the attention, the craft of it, and feel the difference between playing for the prize and playing well.
Sphaira. Greek for ball: Epictetus' image for life's outside things, the dice and the ball we're handed, where the point isn't the ball but how we play it.
Your line: let the ball be the ball. The care goes into the play. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners separate the outcome of a task from the way they do it, and judge their day by the quality of their effort, the way the ball players in this chapter care only about the throwing and catching.
